problemText: A natural resource is something from the natural world that people use. Which of the following is a natural resource?
choices: A bicycle built from metal parts
A plastic bag made in a factory
A computer chip designed by engineers
Coal dug from underground
hints: Natural resources come directly from nature, not made by people in factories.
Think about what the word 'natural' means — does it come from the Earth or from a factory?

problemText: A farmer wants to know whether the water in a river is a renewable or nonrenewable resource. Use the one-question test to classify it. Which answer is correct?
choices: Water is renewable because rain and melting snow refill rivers within a person's lifetime.
Water is nonrenewable because nature takes hundreds of years to cycle water through the atmosphere and back to rivers.
Water is nonrenewable because some rivers run underground and are harder for people to access.
Water is renewable because it has always existed on Earth since before humans lived here.
hints: The one-question test asks: can nature supply a new amount of this resource within a person's lifetime?
Think about the water cycle — how often does nature refill rivers with new water?

problemText: A mining company extracts iron ore from rock deep beneath the ground. How should iron ore be classified, and why?
choices: Renewable, because it comes from deep underground where there is a very large quantity available for mining.
Nonrenewable, because it takes far longer than a person's lifetime for nature to form new iron ore deposits.
Renewable, because ore is a solid material that people can dig up, process, and use for tools and construction.
Nonrenewable, because miners have to use special equipment and dig very deep into the ground to extract it.
hints: Location underground does not decide whether a resource is renewable or nonrenewable.
Ask yourself: after a deposit of iron ore is mined out, how long does it take nature to make a new one?

problemText: Two students are debating whether natural gas is renewable. Student A says, 'Natural gas must be nonrenewable because it comes from underground, just like fossil fuels.' Student B says, 'Natural gas could be renewable because it is a gas, not a solid, so maybe nature can make more of it quickly.' Who is correct, and what is the best explanation?
choices: Student A is correct. All resources found underground are nonrenewable because they must be extracted by mining or drilling.
Student B is correct. Gases are always renewable resources because their form allows them to move and regenerate quickly in nature.
Student A is closer to correct, but for the wrong reason. Natural gas is nonrenewable because it takes far longer than a person's lifetime to form, not just because it is underground.
Neither student used the right method. The classification depends on whether natural gas is burned for energy or stored in tanks.
hints: Recall the worked example with geothermal energy and copper ore — both come from underground but are classified differently.
The one-question test asks about time, not about location or the form of the resource.

problemText: A geothermal power plant uses heat energy from deep inside Earth to produce electricity. Another power plant burns coal for the same purpose. Explain why these two energy sources are classified differently, even though both must be extracted from underground.
choices: Geothermal energy is renewable and coal is nonrenewable because geothermal energy produces electricity more efficiently and with less waste than coal does.
Geothermal energy is renewable and coal is nonrenewable because geothermal energy is found in more locations worldwide than coal deposits are.
Geothermal energy is renewable and coal is nonrenewable because heat travels continuously upward from Earth's interior while coal deposits form only in rare underground conditions.
Geothermal energy is renewable and coal is nonrenewable because Earth keeps producing new geothermal heat within a person's lifetime, but coal takes far longer than a person's lifetime to form.
hints: Remember that location does not decide the classification — only how long nature takes to resupply the resource does.
Apply the one-question test to each one: can nature supply a new amount within a person's lifetime?

problemText: A student reads that oil is pumped from underground, then concludes: 'Since oil is nonrenewable and comes from underground, all underground resources must be nonrenewable.' Test this claim by classifying wind energy and geothermal energy using the one-question test. Which explanation correctly shows why the student's conclusion is wrong?
choices: The student is wrong because geothermal energy is found deep underground and is renewable — nature produces new geothermal heat continuously within a person's lifetime, proving that underground location does not determine the classification.
The student is wrong because wind and geothermal energy are not extracted from underground locations, so the one-question test does not apply to them in the same way as it does to oil.
The student is wrong because wind and geothermal energy are newer technologies that scientists have only recently developed for practical human use and electricity production.
The student is wrong because the one-question test applies only to fossil fuels and mined materials, not to energy sources that come from the sun or from inside Earth.
hints: One contrasting case is enough to disprove a claim that uses 'all' or 'must.' Does geothermal energy fit or break the student's rule?
Look back at the worked example comparing geothermal energy and copper ore — they make the same point about location.

problemText: A student wants to conserve water. She turns off the tap while brushing her teeth instead of letting the water run the whole time. What is this conservation practice called?
choices: Reuse
Reduce
Recycle
Repair
hints: This happens before any water is wasted or thrown away.
The student is choosing to use a smaller amount from the start.

problemText: A library has old wooden chairs that no longer match the new furniture style. Instead of throwing them out, the library donates them to a community center, which sets them up in its game room. The chairs are still solid and work the same way they did before. Which conservation practice does the library's action best describe?
choices: Reduce, because the library is using less furniture than it did before.
Recycle, because the wood from the chairs is being processed into new material.
Reuse, because the same chairs do another job instead of being thrown away.
Repair, because the chairs needed to be fixed before they could be used again.
hints: The same chairs are not broken down or remade into something else.
The identical objects are kept working for a different purpose.

problemText: A restaurant runs out of clean ceramic plates during lunch service. The kitchen crew quickly washes a stack of dirty plates and uses them again to serve more customers that same day. What conservation practice does washing and reusing the plates represent?
choices: Reduce, because the restaurant washes plates instead of ordering new ones.
Repair, because the plates are cleaned to make them work like new.
Recycle, because water is used to clean the plates for a second use.
Reuse, because the same plates do their job again without being replaced.
hints: The identical plates keep serving food, not being broken down into raw material.
Consider whether the plates are doing the same job again or a different job.

problemText: A family uses paper napkins at dinner every night and throws them away after one use. A neighbor suggests that the family could conserve by switching to cloth napkins that are washed and used many times before wearing out. Explain why switching to cloth napkins slows down how quickly the family uses paper resources, even though it does not reduce, reuse, or recycle in the traditional sense.
choices: By using the same cloth napkins repeatedly instead of new paper napkins every night, the family needs far fewer new napkins made from raw material over the same stretch of time.
Cloth napkins reduce the total demand for paper products each year because fewer trees need to be harvested annually to meet the family's napkin needs over time.
Cloth napkins lower the rate of resource consumption because one set of cloth items can serve the same function that would otherwise require many separate paper items purchased repeatedly.
Washing cloth napkins consumes fewer total resources than manufacturing and purchasing new paper napkins would demand from forests and factories throughout the year.
hints: Think about how many new paper napkins would be needed over a month or a year, compared to how many cloth napkins are needed.
The key idea is that the same conserving practice — slowing down how fast people draw on a resource — can work through different mechanisms.

problemText: A toy building block breaks in half and no longer connects properly to other blocks. A child's parent repairs the block by gluing the pieces back together. Compare this to a situation where a child simply stops playing with blocks and asks for video games instead. Only one of these is a conservation practice. Which one is it, and why?
choices: Stopping to play with blocks is the conservation practice because it prevents the family from buying additional plastic toys that would require new material to be manufactured.
Repairing the broken block is the conservation practice because it keeps an already-made item in service longer instead of needing a new block made.
Both are conservation practices because they both result in fewer toys being made and fewer resources used during manufacturing processes.
Neither is a conservation practice because toys have already been manufactured, so the decision about them cannot affect how much new material gets extracted from the earth.
hints: Recall that reduce means using less from the very start, before anything breaks.
Repair applies only to something that has already stopped working, and it matters because the same item can keep doing its job.

problemText: Two students each receive a birthday gift. Student A's gift comes in a plastic clamshell container, which Student A cuts open, throws in the trash, and never uses again. Student B receives a gift in a sturdy cardboard box that can be folded and stored. Student B then uses the same box three times over the next year to pack items when moving to different homes. Neither student recycles or repairs anything. Over the course of one year, which student's choice leads to less new packaging material needing to be made, and which conservation practice explains why?
choices: Student A uses less because avoiding single-use containers counts as reducing material use.
Neither student's choice matters because the packaging has already been made before they received the gifts.
Student B uses less because reusing the same box multiple times means fewer new boxes need to be made to replace it.
Student B uses less because the cardboard box can be broken down and remade, which is a form of recycling.
hints: One new box that does multiple jobs replaces fewer total new boxes than would have been needed otherwise.
Look for the practice where an item that still works gives another job instead of being thrown away.

problemText: An adaptation is a change people make to fit the climate they live in. Which of the following is an example of an adaptation?
choices: Staying indoors during hot days because you prefer cooler temperatures
Moving to a different country because you do not like the current weather
Wearing layers of clothing in a cold climate to trap warm air between them
Buying expensive outdoor gear because it is fashionable
hints: An adaptation solves a problem the climate creates.
Think about something people build, wear, eat, or use to travel that actually fits their climate's conditions.

problemText: A region receives heavy rain for four months each year and experiences widespread flooding in low-lying areas during that season. The ground turns to mud and many roads become impassable. Which form of transportation would work best for this climate?
choices: Large, heavy trucks designed to carry cargo long distances on paved highways
Bicycles, because they are lightweight and do not require fuel
Motorcycles, because they are faster than any other vehicle
Boats and raised walkways that can move people and goods over water and mud
hints: The tough problem here is water and mud covering the ground for part of the year.
Think about what vehicle or path would still work when regular roads flood.

problemText: A climate stays hot and sunny almost every day of the year, with very little rainfall. People who live there wear loose-fitting, lightweight clothing in light colors. Why does this clothing choice fit this climate?
choices: Loose, lightweight clothing lets air move against the skin and light colors reflect sunlight instead of absorbing heat
Light colors make people look fashionable in sunny places, and loose clothing is easier to pack when traveling to hot regions
The clothing dries quickly after washing in the intense sun and the light colors hide dust better in dry climates
Loose fitting garments reduce the amount of fabric needed to make a complete outfit, so people in hot places save money on clothing costs
hints: Focus on how this clothing helps the body release heat, not on appearance or effort.
Think about what happens to heat when air moves against skin and when light colors face sunlight.

problemText: A climate has long, bitter winters with deep snow for several months, and a very short growing season. A house in this climate has thick walls, small windows, and a steep roof. A different climate is hot and humid all year with heavy rain and no winter. Explain why the same house design would fail in the second climate, even though it works well in the first.
choices: Steep roofs shed snow by directing it off the roof quickly, but in a hot, humid climate they would allow too much air circulation and make cooling the house more difficult
Thick walls and small windows hold heat inside, which is helpful when it is cold, but would trap unwanted heat in a climate that is always hot and humid

Small windows limit the size of the rooms inside the house, which works in cold climates where people stay indoors most of the year, but would feel cramped in a warm climate where people want to spend time outside
Thick walls are expensive to build in tropical regions because the materials used for cold climates, such as stone and heavy wood, are scarcer and cost more in places with heavy rain
hints: Consider what problem thick walls and small windows solve in a cold climate.
Now flip it: what would those same features do in a place that is already hot and never needs heat to stay inside?

problemText: A student says, 'People who live in a climate with a very long, cold winter and only a short growing season should eat fresh fruits and vegetables year-round, just like people in warm climates where crops grow most of the year.' What is wrong with this statement, and what food choice would actually fit the cold climate better?
choices: Fresh fruits and vegetables require too much water to grow in cold climates, so people must rely on frozen food and canned goods that do not need water to be stored safely
Fresh food spoils quickly because the warm sun in all climates causes decay at the same rate, so people in cold climates must grow twice as many crops to replace those that rot
The statement ignores that in a long, cold climate very few crops can grow when snow covers the ground, so people need food that can be stored for months, such as dried food
Growing fresh food year-round is possible only in regions near the equator, so people living far from the equator must trade with tropical nations to receive shipped vegetables
hints: Think about what 'long, cold winter' means for how long crops can actually grow in the ground.
If crops cannot grow for many months, what kind of food do people need so they have enough to eat?

problemText: Two neighboring regions have very different climates. Region X has a long, cold, snowy winter and a short, mild summer. Region Y is hot and humid year-round with heavy seasonal rain. Compare how housing, clothing, and food storage would need to be different in these two regions. Then explain why a person who moved from Region X to Region Y could not use the same adaptations that worked in their original home.
choices: Region X uses thick walls and heavy clothing to survive cold winters, but Region Y stays warm year-round so these same designs would trap excessive heat and make living conditions uncomfortably warm

Region X stores dried and preserved food using techniques suited to long dry winters because crops grow only a few months each year, while Region Y can grow fresh crops year-round due to continuous warmth and seasonal rain, making preservation methods unnecessary and less practical for the climate

Region Y needs stored dried food and heavy winter clothing just like Region X does because all regions must prepare for a cold season by using the same preservation and clothing strategies, even if that cold season never actually occurs in that particular location

Region X needs thick-walled houses, heavy layered clothing, and stored dried food, while Region Y needs open-sided houses, loose light clothing, and can rely on fresh food year-round, because the cold and snow in Region X require very different solutions than the heat and rain in Region Y
hints: List what problem each region's climate creates: cold/snow versus heat/water.
Now ask: does the same solution work for both? Would thick walls help in a hot, humid place?

problemText: Natural resources are distributed unevenly across Earth. This means that some places have large amounts of a particular resource while other places have very little or none of that same resource. Based on this definition of resource distribution, which statement is true?
choices: Fertile soil, thick forest, and mineral deposits each follow their own separate pattern of where they are found in large amounts.
Every place on Earth has the same amount of fertile soil, thick forest, and mineral deposits in equal proportions.
A place that has one type of natural resource in large amounts must also have equally large amounts of all other types of natural resources in the same location.
Resource distribution describes how quickly resources can be transported from one place to another and how fast they can be processed.
hints: Think about what 'uneven' means — are the patterns of different resources the same everywhere?
One pattern (fertile soil) does not predict another pattern (forest or minerals).

problemText: A region has deep, fertile soil and steady rainfall but very few trees. Based only on these facts about the region's resources, which large-scale activity would be most difficult to support there?
choices: Large-scale crop farming, because farming needs steady rainfall and fertile soil to grow.
Large-scale logging, because logging depends on having enough trees to cut.
Large-scale fishing, because the region has water resources available.
Large-scale mining, because mining depends on access to mineral deposits underground.
hints: Look at what each activity depends on to work at a large scale.
The region has very few trees — does logging have what it needs?

problemText: Town Riverside has a large mineral deposit in the ground and access to clean water. Which statement best explains why Riverside's resources would support large-scale mining?
choices: Mining requires clean water more than any other resource, and Riverside has it in large amounts available for industrial use.
Mining is the only economic activity that can succeed in a town with mineral deposits, so Riverside must be suited to mining.
Mining depends on having a concentrated amount of valuable mineral to dig out, which Riverside has underground.
Any town with water access can mine minerals from the ground no matter what else is present or where the minerals are located.
hints: What does mining actually need to do its work — what does it depend on?
A mineral deposit is a concentrated amount of valuable mineral built up in one place.

problemText: Town Blackstone has thick forest and thin, rocky soil. A student claims: 'Blackstone's resources are not as good as a town with fertile land, because you cannot farm there.' Explain the error in this claim and correct it, using only facts about what each type of land suits.
choices: The claim is wrong because it compares one type of land to another without checking what activities each type actually suits best. The correct statement is that Blackstone's thick forest and rocky soil are poor for farming but well-suited to logging, a different activity than the fertile land supports.

The claim is wrong because thin, rocky soil prevents farming but does not prevent all economic activity in a town. The correct statement is that Blackstone can rely on logging and forest products since its forest resource is thick, even though its soil prevents large-scale crop production.

The claim is wrong because it assumes that all resources must be ranked by whether they can support farming as the main activity. The correct statement is that Blackstone's forest is suited to logging while fertile land is suited to farming — different activities that cannot be ranked as better or worse.

The claim wrongly ranks Blackstone's land as 'not as good' by comparing one activity. The correct statement is that Blackstone's thick forest suits large-scale logging, while fertile land suits large-scale farming — each suits a different activity, not a better or worse one.
hints: Is ranking one type of land 'better' than another a geography question, or does it assume something that goes beyond just describing resources?
What activity does thick forest suit, and what activity does fertile land suit? Are they ranked, or just different?

problemText: Region A has wide, flat, fertile land with steady rainfall and very few mineral deposits. Region B has poor soil but large mineral deposits in the ground. A student writes: 'Region A is better than Region B because Region A can farm and Region B cannot.' Using the concept that a place missing one resource still has others that suit different activities, explain why this ranking is misleading.
choices: The ranking is misleading because Region A's ability to farm does not make it 'better' overall; Region B's mineral deposit suits large-scale mining instead, a different activity that Region A cannot support as well. Neither place is ranked better — each suits a different activity.

The ranking is misleading because Region B can actually farm if it has access to irrigation and fertilizers, which means both regions can farm equally and Region A should not be ranked higher than Region B.

The ranking is misleading because it ignores that Region B has a valuable resource in its mineral deposits that suits mining, a major economic activity that Region A cannot perform as well even though Region A can farm.
The ranking is misleading because Region A's flat terrain makes it harder to farm than sloped land, so Region B with its poor soil should actually be ranked higher for its farming potential.
hints: Just because Region B cannot farm, does that mean it has no useful resources?
What activity does Region B's resource suit, even if Region A's resource suits a different activity?

problemText: Two towns, both with thick forest, were compared by a student: 'Town Pine has thick forest and is suited to logging. Town Oak also has thick forest but has very different soil and rainfall than Pine. Yet Oak must also be suited to logging exactly like Pine is, because they both have the same forest resource.' Identify the error in this reasoning and explain what you would need to know about Town Oak to determine whether its resources really suit large-scale logging.
choices: The error is that two towns with the same forest resource will always be suited to the same activities regardless of other conditions. You would need to know whether Town Oak's forest is the same age as Pine's forest to tell if logging will work equally well there.

The error is assuming that having one matching resource means all the other conditions for an activity are also the same. To determine whether Oak's resources really suit large-scale logging, you would need to know whether Oak has enough trees that can actually be cut — just having forest is not enough if the trees are too small, too scattered, or too difficult to access.

The error is that forests in different towns are never suited to logging under any circumstances, no matter what conditions exist. You would need to know the total population of Town Oak to determine whether logging could work there.

The error is that the student did not account for the fact that rainfall patterns are more important than forest for logging success. You would need to know Town Oak's rainfall amounts and patterns to see if logging is possible.
hints: Does having a resource in the ground automatically mean an activity will succeed, or does the resource need to be usable in a certain way?
Large-scale logging depends on having enough trees to cut — what would 'enough' actually mean in practice?
